abstract: Methods of determining plant anatomy often rely on time-consuming preparation techniques and targeted sampling of tissues of assumed importance. This typically involves single plane 2D examination over small profiles of sub-sampled plant tissue with limited ability for 3D extrapolation of internal anatomies of plant organs. This limitation can create phenotyping bottlenecks. These bottlenecks are particularly acute in plant species that are larger than commonly used model systems, which have typically been selected for their small size and suitability for high-density growth. Many major crop species, by contrast, are larger and have more complex internal structures. In this paper, we investigated whether X-ray computed tomography (XCT) provides an effective means of overcoming this phenotyping bottleneck, using the barley stem as a model system. Sample preparation approaches and scan parameters were compared. The resulting datasets were evaluated for qualitative observation and quantitative analyses of targeted volumetric structures. We demonstrate that plant samples suitable for XCT can be prepared without extended preparation times or toxic contrast agents. Freeze-drying provided cellular-resolution imaging of mature, structurally robust tissues, whereas critical point drying provided more reliable preservation of soft tissues undergoing active development. We then show how high-resolution scan data can be used to measure anatomical features in three dimensions, generate radial attenuation profiles, and extract computationally segmented models of isolated anatomical features. The scanning and analysis methods described here provide a means of recovering plant anatomy across multiple spatial scales in 3D digital reconstructions, providing routes to quantitative phenotyping in comparisons between different accessions, growth regimes, and mutants.
